title: Cibeles House / Taller Síntesis
text:
Cibeles House / Taller Síntesis

The Cibeles House is located in the municipality of La Ceja, a region characterized by open landscapes, gentle topography, and a strong presence of native vegetation. This natural setting not only frames the project but also defines its starting point: conceiving a home that respects the site, reduces its footprint, and allows the landscape to maintain its continuity.

title: Claranet Portugal Headquarters / PROMONTORIO
text:
Claranet Portugal Headquarters / PROMONTORIO

Claranet is an IT company providing network hosting and managed application services (Hybrid Cloud Hosting) to corporate clients across Europe and Brazil. The practice was invited to design its Portuguese headquarters on the site of a former military depot, itself built on the grounds of the 17th-century Grilas Sisters' convent. The convent survived the 1755 earthquake but not the 1834 extinction of the religious orders. It became state property and in 1897, was converted into military warehouses. After the 2016 Web Summit, the city rescued it to create Lisbon's International Innovation Hub, now a group of municipal concession buildings for tech-based services and creative industries.

title: CS3 - Event & Sports Pavilion / HA+MA
text:
CS3 - Event & Sports Pavilion / HA+MA

CS3 is an Event and Sports Pavilion situated in Los Angeles, CA. Constructed of mass timber, the structure offers a variety of spaces and facilities for sports, outdoor activities, social events and food service.

title: Grande Nef de l'Île-des-Vannes Renovation / Chatillon Architectes
text:
Grande Nef de l'Île-des-Vannes Renovation / Chatillon Architectes

Following seven years of closure, Chatillon Architectes implements contemporary solutions and state-of-the-art facilities, bringing this distinctive building back to life, first as an Olympic training site and then for its subsequent return to the local community. The first images of the restored Grande Nef de l'Île-des-Vannes sports complex in Paris have been revealed ahead of its role as an Olympic training facility. Featuring a sweeping parabolic roof and striking translucent side paneling, the unique structure was designed by Anatole Kopp, Lucien Metrich, and Pierre Chazanoff in 1971, and closed in 2018 due to decay and accessibility issues. Adapting the building for contemporary use, Chatillon Architectes has fully restored the structure, installing contemporary energy solutions, structural repairs, universal accessibility upgrades and state-of-the-art facilities, from acoustic paneling to sports flooring to lighting fixtures.

title: House WE / Wespi de Meuron Romeo architects

House WE / Wespi de Meuron Romeo architects

title: Form Follows Formation: How Architecture Works with Geological Shapes
text:
Form Follows Formation: How Architecture Works with Geological Shapes

A canyon is a space no one designed. Its walls expose layers of rock deposited over millions of years, and the passage between them exists because water slowly wore that rock away. Glaciers shaped valleys in a similar way, leaving slopes behind as the ice retreated. Long before architects began shaping spaces, the Earth was already producing them.

title: Resort Nasima / Studio Madouh
text:
Resort Nasima / Studio Madouh

Resort Nasima is part of a residential development throughout the State of Kuwait. The form of this resort delivers a fluid journey throughout the premises, circulating between 3 independent units, which was inspired by natural sea-to-stone erosion.

title: What is Modified Wood? How Technology Is Expanding What Wood Can Do
text:
What is Modified Wood? How Technology Is Expanding What Wood Can Do

Wood has been used in buildings for thousands of years. It is natural, renewable and versatile, but its response to moisture requires consideration in design and specification. Changing moisture conditions can cause it to swell and shrink, while prolonged moisture exposure can create conditions for fungal decay. Historically, using wood outdoors has therefore meant choosing naturally durable species, protecting the material or designing around the way wood behaves. Wood modification offers another approach: changing certain properties of the material itself.

title: RAMSA Unveils Plans for New Welcome Hall at Chicago’s Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
text:
RAMSA Unveils Plans for New Welcome Hall at Chicago’s Griffin Museum of Science and Industry

RAMSA (Robert A.M. Stern Architects) has unveiled the design for a new Welcome Hall at the Kenneth C. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry (Griffin MSI) in Chicago, Illinois. The project involves reopening the building's historic North Portico as a year-round entrance and introducing a new glazed volume connecting the portico to the museum's exhibition spaces. The proposal is part of a master plan completed by RAMSA in 2024 that examines the use of the museum's existing exhibition and public areas.

title: Pamiškio House / ARCHISPEKTRAS
text:
Pamiškio House / ARCHISPEKTRAS

One of the primary objectives in designing Pamiškio House was to strike a balance between privacy and an open dialogue with nature. Set within a remarkable landscape of forest, river, and sloping terrain, the house seeks to embrace its surroundings while maintaining clear boundaries that provide a sense of security, intimacy, and retreat.

title: From Asbestos to Fungi: Eight New Materials Made from Waste and Living Matter
text:
From Asbestos to Fungi: Eight New Materials Made from Waste and Living Matter

Architecture is, above all, a material reality. The materials that surround us are the result of a chain of constructive, economic, aesthetic and, in more contemporary examples, environmental considerations. Decisions are shaped by available technology, manageable technique, time-related expectations and regulatory frameworks. To face the pressures on our built environment, those multidimensional conditions must change through what we call innovation: the tangible creation of new products and strategies with problem-solving capabilities. Matter is the general term for physical substance that has mass and takes up space. When matter is given a specific type, form, or useful application, it becomes material. Material transformation therefore requires going beyond recycling and reuse: combining existing matter to create new materials that open up new possibilities for construction. The research presented below suggests that demonizing existing materials is unnecessary as long as this capacity for innovation exists.

title: Dammed Between Energy and Water Scarcity: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and the Nile
text:
Dammed Between Energy and Water Scarcity: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and the Nile

Every large dam divides as much as it connects, and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is no exception. A monumental feat of architecture and engineering, the mega-dam has brought everyone together, for better or worse, to interrogate who gets to declare sovereignty over the riches of the river, be it water or momentum, and to challenge colonial-era Nile treaties.

title: Casa 9 / Hoang GK
text:
Casa 9 / Hoang GK

Designed as a psychological retreat for urban families, Casa 9 is a private weekend retreat where the boundaries between people, living spaces, and tropical nature dissolve. The design draws on a boldly spreading A-frame roof as the primary shelter for the entire house. Its tall, double-layered pitched roof and extended eaves form an effective thermal buffer, minimizing direct solar heat gain while casting broad shade over the living spaces below.

title: Village de Ananti / SKM Architects
text:
Village de Ananti / SKM Architects

Set on a sloping seaside site in Gijang-gun, Busan, Village de Ananti is a 392-room leisure and cultural complex that brings together the calm of the sea and forest with the energy of urban life. The project covers 160,324 m² of land framed by the ocean and wooded hills, with a total floor area of approximately 162,070 m².

title: Casa Cardona  / Sensacional Dinámica Mexicana
text:
Casa Cardona / Sensacional Dinámica Mexicana

Initially conceived as a conventional 165 m² real estate development, the residence demonstrates how an architectural proposal can transcend commercial parameters to create spatial, cultural, and human value. Its architecture establishes an intimate dialogue with the desert, transforming the conditions of its surroundings into a distinctive domestic experience.

title: MMR House / David Ito Arquitetura
text:
MMR House / David Ito Arquitetura

The MMR House was designed for a young couple who brought several highly specific demands to the project. Among them were the desire for a spiral staircase inside the house, the presence of a tree integrated into the interior environment, the ability to see the slope of the roof from the inside, and the creation of a double-height space. In addition, there were general programmatic requirements: four suites, an office, spacious social areas prepared to host around forty people, strong integration with nature, and, at the same time, privacy from the gated community.

title: Santa Rosa Social Housing / FAR frohn&rojas
text:
Santa Rosa Social Housing / FAR frohn&rojas

In recent decades, rising land prices have pushed much of Santiago's social housing to the urban periphery, creating settlements that are often disconnected from social and technical infrastructure.

title: Coqueira House / Tiago Sousa Arquitecto
text:
Coqueira House / Tiago Sousa Arquitecto

Geometry, planes and a suspended volume. The site is organised into two distinct levels. The upper level comprises the majority of the site and is accessed via the upper road. The lower level, on the other hand, is the result of an excavation, connected to the lower road, and is a flat platform contained between large granite retaining walls.

title: Ironwood Retreat / The Ranch Mine
text:
Ironwood Retreat / The Ranch Mine

Most of Arizona's streams run only after a storm. Oak Creek is one of the few that flows all year and the water changes everything around it. Along its banks in Sedona, Arizona, sycamores, cottonwoods, ash and alder grow into a canopy of shade and green that most of the state never sees. On a wooded bend of the creek, architecture firm The Ranch Mine has designed "Ironwood," a small retreat built around one simple wish: to spend the days and nights down by the water, under the trees.

title: Dondoh Restaurant / Costa + Herrera Arquitectos
text:
Dondoh Restaurant / Costa + Herrera Arquitectos

Dondoh is Chile's first Japanese grill. This venue, recently opened in the Chilean capital, stands out for its imposing design inspired by Japan's ancient Izakayas. Elements such as wood, stone, and fire serve as the main protagonists. Dondoh refers to an ancient Japanese ceremony performed by farmers around the year 1500, invoking the God of Fire. The God of Fire would warm the Earth so that seeds could germinate. The fire was fed with small wooden tablets, and the flames rose along with the prayers written upon them.

title: MOKUZAI / IT'S Studio
text:
MOKUZAI / IT'S Studio

Mokuzai is an office building that includes public health services, featuring a mixed timber and concrete structure designed by IT'S.

title: The City as a Quarry: Housing Transformation
text:
The City as a Quarry: Housing Transformation

The City as a Quarry: Housing Transformation brings together representatives of the European Commission and the Government of Catalonia with European architects to explore how the renovation, reuse and transformation of existing buildings can help increase housing supply in response to the housing crisis and the climate emergency.

Curated by architects Marta Peris and José Toral of PERIS+TORAL Arquitectes, the event examines the conversion of offices and commercial premises, the renovation and extension of residential buildings, and the reuse of structures and materials. Discussions will address public policy, financing, regulation and architectural practice.

The event is part of the series Contemporary Catalan

title: Planned Overflow: How Singapore Balances Floods, Canals, and Public Space
text:
Planned Overflow: How Singapore Balances Floods, Canals, and Public Space

At Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park in Singapore, a river does not occupy a fixed boundary. Under ordinary conditions, water moves through a naturalized channel bordered by grass, planting, and paths that bring visitors close to the river. During heavy rainfall, water spreads into the surrounding park, which is designed to accommodate flows beyond the capacity of the narrower channel. What appears to be a public landscape is also working infrastructure. Singapore's approach retains drainage engineering while assigning a wider role to the land around it.

title: Going nowhere fast
text:
Going nowhere fast

When speed disguises itself as progress.

I distinctly remember my father driving the speed limit down a two-way street in the Bronx when a car swung out from behind us and cut into our lane with a few feet to spare. It wasn’t the first time, and whenever it happened, I’d anticipate his favorite phrase, delivered with zero road rage, “Going nowhere fast.”

Twenty seconds later, we rolled up to a red light, with the car that cut us off sitting right next to us. One question that stayed with me as a curious 12-year-old: “Did they notice?” Did the driver notice that, after all that effort to get ahead, their reward was a red light? Did speed feel like progress to them?

Speed that feels like progress

Drivers act on the information they have and make quick decisions. Empty lane. I can go around and make the next light. The reality is that many traffic lights run on a timed sequence. Beating one light will often get you to the next red light sooner. The driver who cut us off will almost always remember the pass, not the light. The cost will not appear where the shortcut was taken, but will show up later. By then it’ll be easy to miss what caused it.

Today, product teams are in that lane. For decades we’ve leaned on a tidy rule, GIGO (garbage in, garbage out). It assumed the garbage was obvious. With AI, it isn’t. Garbage goes in and comes out polished, making “beating the system” look like winning. AI can’t weigh what’s true for your users; it predicts what’s likely. Feed it your own data (interview notes, support tickets, instrumentation data), and the polish has truth underneath it. Feed it a guess, and it’ll output a guess with confidence.

Atlassian’s State of Product 2026 report found that product managers gain nearly two hours a day with AI, yet most still feel stuck in reactive mode, and 84% have concerns their products won’t succeed. Speed increased. Confidence did not. Faster output isn’t the same as assurance that you’re building the right thing.

When AI takes the wheel

Drivers who cut through traffic are under pressure, and an opening looks like an opportunity. Starting with AI works the same way. Ask it for user needs, customer experience maps, and personas, and you’ll have results in minutes. Results that can leave you with false confidence that you’ve found the exact problem you’re solving for. Defining a problem solely within an LLM’s capabilities lets AI do the heavy lifting based on averages, preexisting biases, and general patterns of what’s been written about the thing you’re trying to solve. And the output is often opaque, forcing teams to trace back why conclusions emerged or what assumptions shaped them, frequently hitting a dead end.

This is top-down thinking, and it doesn’t address your customer’s pain today. Relying on AI before meaningful design discovery can be tremendously costly. It eats up engineering and design time, causes organizational toil for product teams, and creates disruptions that show up much later. In high-stakes areas like hiring, fintech, lending, and healthcare, it can cause great harm.

Bottom-up thinking begins with humans. It involves research to define a problem and understand the systems connected to it, with all of their interdependent parts. It’s messy work, like mapping how a need links to complex networks and processes orbiting around it. It let’s teams be wrong early, when it’s cheap. It’s a route that unpacks what’s unique and specific to your users. This is where AI becomes useful, by processing your users’ needs once you’ve observed them.

The synthetic research trap

In Thinking in Systems, Donella Meadows unpacks a trap called ‘rule beating’, following the letter of a rule to circumvent its purpose.

She highlights this with a Calvin and Hobbes strip by Bill Watterson:

In the comic strip, Calvin tells Hobbes he’ll do ten good deeds daily until Christmas so Santa goes easy on him. When Hobbes points out Susie (his nemesis) is “coming this way,” Calvin decides he’ll start tomorrow and do twenty a day.

Calvin isn’t trying to be benevolent. He hopes to catch up on a year of bad behavior to look good for Santa.

Synthetic research (AI-generated) participants can work the same way. One of the most widely cited principles in UX and human-centered design is to understand your users before you build. Synthetic personas let teams check the research box without meeting a single user.

“Research isn’t just about avoiding the average. It’s the only way to get the newest answer.”

When NN/g re-ran three of its own studies using AI-generated participants, it found the answers were too shallow to be helpful. In one study, the synthetic participants claimed they had completed each course. The research looked complete, but the answers were too good to be true.

In a 2026 User Interviews survey of 150 researchers, 81% used AI regularly in their work, but only 8% used it to simulate participants. Their biggest concerns were the quality and accuracy of insights (88%) and stakeholders overly trusting AI-generated findings (79%).

The newest answer lives in the field.

Your users’ behavior is the newest and truest information that you have. Their workarounds from last month, the rage clicks that began after the last release, net new needs that started to bubble up this quarter after industry shifts. They exist only in the field. Your product’s newest nuances won’t reliably surface in any training data. Research isn’t just about avoiding the average. It’s the only way to get the newest answer.

Meadows’ way out isn’t adding more rules. It’s redesigning them so that people’s efforts go toward the goal instead of around it. For product teams, it means measuring whether we understand our users, not whether we produced a persona or archetype. A research finding can trace back to something tangible, an interview or a support ticket.

What discovery can reveal

Consider a product team asked to speed up the permissions workflow in an admin console. To move quickly, they prompt AI to create an admin persona. The persona is convincing; busy, technical, and frustrated by too many clicks.

The obvious solution follows:
1. Bulk actions
2. Fewer confirmations
3. Single click to apply changes across the organization

Then a designer, PM, and developer spend a week with five real admins, and a completely different theme emerges. They want to move faster, but speed isn’t their biggest worry. Mistakes are. One wrong change can lock hundreds of people out of their tools or give the wrong group access to sensitive information.

They don’t need fewer steps. What they need is confidence:
• A preview of who a change will affect
• A record of what changed and when
• An easy and clear way to undo

With these in place, bulk actions stop being a risk and become the speedup that the team asked for.

The AI persona wasn’t wrong that administrators are busy. It was average. It described what admins in general say, not what these administrators risk. Building on personas alone, the team would have shipped a faster way to make costly mistakes, and found out months later through support escalations and lost trust.

Discovery did not slow the team down. It gave AI detail to work with. Once the team had transcripts and a quarter’s worth of support tickets, the LLM ranked failure scenarios, drafted audit-log requirements, and generated concepts for previews and undo flows. With the same LLM, the input was now grounded in what actual customers are experiencing. As a result, they built something the admin (at the center of their product) actually values.

“…your competitors don’t have exactly what your users told you”

Discovery and research first, then accelerate

Speed is never the problem. Rule beating is. Once humans have begun the work, AI becomes a powerful accelerator. It synthesizes interview notes, spots patterns, generates concept variations, and sharpens questions you can bring to the next round of research. The difference is that it’s working from your users.

Discovery gives you two advantages over teams racing toward the next light:

  1. You stay out of their pileup: Unvalidated work drains teams with costly rework, organizational toil, and disruption after shipping a feature. Teams doing discovery aren’t in that collision.
  2. You expose their blind spot and see what they can’t: Every competitor has access to the same models, and anyone can quickly spin up a product spec and render an outcome in seconds. The real advantage is that your competitors don’t have exactly what your users told you.

To this day, my father has never won a race to a red light. He’s also never been in an accident. Decades of driving throughout the metro area, and not a single pileup. He isn’t slow. He just knows how the road works.

Real leverage today doesn’t come from flooring it with every new AI capability. It comes from anchoring the tool to what you’ve learned from your users and understanding the road beneath you. That’s how you get where you’re actually trying to go, and take your customers with you.

They will notice.

Originally published October 19th, 2026
Over the past decade, I’ve focused on designing product experiences for developers within multidisciplinary teams. I’ve led design for IaC adoption, incident management, and observability within socio-technical environments.

title: Building an AI-ready design system library: Code → Figma with MCP.
text:
Building an AI-ready design system library: Code → Figma with MCP.

In-System Design

A practical guide for designers: why my design system starts in code, and how I build, check and maintain the Figma library.

In-System Design: a three-part series.
Part 1: Building an AI-ready design system: Code → Figma (you are here)
Part 2: AI prototyping inside your design system (3 November 2026)
Part 3: From code to Figma and back (10 November 2026)

For designers who know Figma well and have never written production code, and for the design system teams around them. Every technical word is explained in the box at the end.

For most of my career, the work went one way. I designed in Figma, a developer turned it into code, and when something did not survive the trip, we sorted it out between us.

Then I handed that same route to an AI, and what came back was unsettling, mainly because it looked fine. It read my Figma file, translated it faithfully, and filled in everything the file did not say with whatever seemed plausible.

The code that comes out is mediocre, and that is the part everyone frets about. Fair enough, since code quality is at least the part you can read, review and complain about in a pull request.

What worries me more is what gets invented: the focus order, the error states, what a screen reader announces, what happens when a request fails, or when a list comes back empty. None of that shows up in a screenshot, so nobody catches it in review.

So I turned the direction around. My design system now starts in code, and I generate my Figma library from it. Code always wins, and Figma is a mirror, not a second truth.

That sounds like a demotion for Figma, and in practice my Figma file got busier. This article is why, how I build the library, and how I keep an existing one honest, including the parts that still need babysitting.

Why doesn’t Figma-to-code with AI work well?

Because your Figma file was always supposed to be an abstraction. Let me explain: I sat down one afternoon and compared what a React component can express with what a Figma component can express, because that is the kind of thing I do for fun now, apparently. The life and soul of the party, I am. My count came out at roughly 17% coverage. For CSS, it was better, around 45%, and still nowhere near complete.

Those are my own numbers from my own comparison, not an official statistic. Check them against your own stack before quoting them in a meeting.

Everything Figma cannot say used to be filled in by a developer who could walk over and ask a question.

That gap is not a Figma failure, and no, I do not want Figma to close it. If focus order, container behaviour and ARIA labels lived in the file, you would need to be a front-end developer to use your own library.

A developer also notices what is missing. An AI does not. It takes the file literally, as a complete instruction, fills the gaps with whatever it has seen most often, and carries on, so the old direction now produces a component that looks finished and is partly invented.

Turn the arrow around and the same literal-mindedness becomes a gift. Generating from code, “it reads exactly what is there” is precisely what you want, because what is there is the real thing: real props, real values, real defaults, real states.

Flip it: Code as the source of truth, Figma follows

Code is the source of truth. Figma mirrors it. Where they differ, Figma is wrong.

I know how that lands in a room full of designers. Designers still do not work in code, and I have no plans to write production code myself. Figma does not matter less either. I think best on a canvas; I design there, and I would fight anyone who tried to take it away, so hear me out.

Hands-on: from a repo to a Figma library, step by step:

This is the workflow I currently use and demo, with the prompts I actually use. You don’t need to be a developer for this. You do need to be comfortable opening a repo and reading what’s in it, and the AI will walk you through the rest. So yes, some new territory, but stay with me! It’s great fun!

What you need:
1. A design system in code you can access, with Storybook running on it
2. An empty Figma file
3. MCP connection. I use and recommend Figma Console MCP by Southleft for this because it reads and writes variables properly, which the basic connection does not.

1. Get access to the code as a designer

A branch, a sandbox, or a playground repo. Ask development for the smallest safe thing: a copy where nothing you do can reach production.

If you want to practise first, download any sample design system as a zip and point your AI at the folder. I hand out a sample file for trainings and sessions, but you can also make your own. Connect that folder or branch with your AI. I will use Claude Code for my example. Your developers will most likely use the terminal or an editor; I use the Claude desktop app and the Claude Code tab.

2. Check that Storybook is there

Once you are connected, ask Claude Code to open Storybook for you.

What you get is a local website: it runs on your own machine, at an address like localhost:6001. Only you can see it, nothing is published, and it is built from the code sitting in front of you. It shows every component, live and clickable.

Storybook does not keep its own copy of your system; it lives inside it. Next to each component sits a small stories file listing its examples, so the page you click through is built from the real code and you can see, understand and compare it as a designer. That is also the key to prototyping with AI and generating sensible output, and I will come back to it in another article.

It is so great to finally go through the real stuff visually as a designer; I cannot believe I didn’t use this earlier! You can look at the Storybook of one of my samples here.

No Storybook? You can still do everything in this article. What you lose is the view and the component list, which I personally need to understand and compare, and for some parity checks later on.

If you are in a playground environment, you can just ask Claude to add it to your own copy and play there. In a real repo, it is a developer’s call, because it brings dependencies somebody has to maintain, so ask rather than install. It also needs to be Storybook 10 or newer, with the components manifest switched on, before an agent can read that list (this is for parity checks and prototyping later).

3. Open an empty Figma file

Clean, empty, and destined to become the library. Not your existing library, which comes later. Then open the Console MCP inside it.

From here, Claude Code is the hub between the two: one arm in the real code, one in the open Figma file. I can ask in plain words for something to be read on one side and built on the other.

4. Tokens and styles first, always

Components use tokens, so the tokens and text styles have to exist before the components do.

First find out where the tokens live, and yes, you can just ask Claude. In my repo they are JSON: one layer of raw values, one of semantic roles. In yours they might be CSS custom properties, or a Tailwind config, in which case I am sorry. Figma then splits them into two: colours, spacing and radii become variables, typography becomes text styles bound to variables. Console MCP does this well; you still have to check it, and you still need to know your way around Figma properly.

My prompt for this step, roughly as I say it:

I want an exact mirror of this repo in Figma. The MCP is on and the file is empty. Let’s do this step by step. Transfer the tokens first. Always use the same naming as the code, so Figma and the code match. Set up collections that match the code, primitives and semantic. Alias them. Scope them. Where needed use modes (e.g. light and dark mode). Do the same for the text styles, using the naming from code, and use variables as in the code. Anything you cannot express, write into GAPS.md always. Then stop and tell me if you need anything.

You will need to adapt this to your setup; mine is React with tokens in JSON, two layers. Once done, check in Figma that everything is set up correctly and compare with Storybook (I ask it to display all of this on a page for me).

5. Build two components as a test

Not the whole system. Two, ideally one simple and one awkward. I use Button and Alert, or some sort of dropdown; it’s fun with Figma.

Now build the Alert and the Button component as a test, set up as in code, using my variables and styles. Anything you cannot express, write into GAPS.md always (GAPS.md I explain below; it’s the best part!).

Then I go and look properly: are the variants complete, are the properties named as in code, is auto layout set up, are the tokens bound and scoped, did it carry the description across.

That last part is where the real value sits. The two sides do not only look alike, they carry the same names and the same properties, down to the spelling. No danger on one side and error on the other, no Card that is secretly a Panel. Everything that comes later in an AI workflow stands on that: prototyping with real components, checking for drift, sending a screen back to code.

If the two come out right, I run the whole library. And yes, that costs time and tokens. However, only once. Staying in sync afterwards is a different job: a contract, or in my case a parity check comparing two JSON lists. More on that soon.

6. Know what you need! Context travels with each element, like a little parcel

You might have heard that context is key when working with AI design systems, especially later as we want to prototype with all of this stuff. Most of what gets called context is a markdown file: a DESIGN.md, a rules file, a page of guidelines. But most of the context is baked into the things themselves. Every token, every component, every style: think of each one as a little parcel carrying its own context.

What is in the parcel:

  • the component name, identical on both sides
  • each property with its allowed values and its default
  • each token name, what it points at, and where it is allowed to be used at all
  • the description written once in code and carried into the Figma component
  • the code syntax on a Figma variable, so the variable knows what it is called in CSS
  • a link back to that component’s page in Storybook
  • and the gaps file, for everything that could not make the trip

None of that was typed into a document by hand, and to be honest, by hand I wouldn’t even get close. Markdown is for the why and the when, the rules and the exceptions. Everything factual gets generated and attached, and then it cannot quietly disagree with the code. Oh, how I love my MCP!

7. Ask for the gaps, every single time via GAPS.md

You might have noticed that I ask for GAPS.md every single time. I ended up with this one by accident. I wanted to know what had happened to all the things Figma could not express, so I asked the AI to list them, and the list turned out to be more useful than the components it had just built.

Write a GAPS.md: everything you could not express in Figma, everything you were unsure about, and anything I should check by hand.

The gaps exist whether or not anyone writes them down, and written down they become reviewable. My own gaps file contains things like line heights that are unitless in code and have to become pixels in Figma, states that only exist in behaviour, and layout rules Figma has no equivalent for. Each one with a note on what I decided. I also include a list of items the AI was unsure about that need my revision.

A gaps file turns the imperfect mirror into a list you can take to a developer and work through, and you might come up with more creative ideas on how to use it.

8. Turn what you learned into a skill

By the third run you will notice you are typing the same corrections. That is the moment to make a skill: a packaged set of instructions your AI loads automatically for this kind of job.

Mine creates tokens and components, writes the gaps file, expects Storybook, then screenshots each generated component and compares it against the matching Storybook story, and compares manifests (a check I use later for parity). It exists because of my own mistakes, and I update it most weeks.

One safety note, because I am asked this every time: a skill can run code on your machine. Make your own as a team or install them, but only from people you trust; read them, or have a developer look first or at least ask Claude to run through it before installing. Installing a random skill because it sounded handy is the same move as opening the “you have won a million” attachment.

Keeping code and Figma parity

Generating the library once is the easy part. Keeping it true as the code changes week after week is the open problem, in my setup and in the industry generally.

So I built myself a little parity checker and keep it as a status page inside Storybook; you can check it out here on my sync status page. You don’t need a page; you need a check, but I am a designer, so I need to see things visually.

How it works, in three steps, quite unspectacular:

  1. Storybook can automatically write a component list. If you are using the Storybook MCP, it generates a file (JSON) called a manifest: every component, its properties, the allowed values and the defaults, straight out of the code. I only found it because of prototyping, where that short list is what makes AI prototyping work at all, since the agent reads the list instead of your whole repo. Which, by the way, is what got me into this whole setup in the first place, as I was so frustrated with the code output of AI builders when prototyping.
  2. So I asked Figma for the same thing. With the MCP open, I had Claude write me a matching list of what is really in my library: same components, same properties, same values. You can see the Figma JSON file I use here.
  3. Then I ran the two against each other. Name against name, property against property, default against default. Everything that matches turns green, anything that moved turns red. Easy!

Both lists are JSON, which is just a text file where every value has a label, so a machine can compare them without interpreting anything.

That comparison is deterministic, and that is exactly what we want: same input, same answer, every time, with no AI in it. The AI only kicks it off in my setup. The downside of mine is that I still have to trigger it by hand, and a real team would have a more sophisticated setup that runs automatically on every change. But very few teams have that right now.

However, building it taught me more than reading about it ever did. I now have a much better idea of what my developers mean when they talk about checks, and I can sit in that conversation and help shape the workflow with design needs in mind.

Side note: Right now it only checks the architecture, the names, properties, allowed values, and defaults. Not the visual side, no CSS. I am working on that.
Another side note: I initially called this a contract, but it isn’t. A contract sits above both sides and both get built from it. Mine compares two sides, and code wins every time, so the honest name is a parity check.

“But I already have a Figma library. Can I update it with MCP? ”

Most teams have one, often with years of work in it. The same connection can compare instead of create.

I take a component I know is out of step, and I ask:

In my open Figma file there is an Alert. Check it against the Alert in the code. This is a library file, so instances depend on it. Think it through with me: would a change list next to it be best, or should you generate a reference version from code next to it so I can compare, or do you want to propose a direct fix? Tell me here in the chat and add this as a visual note in Figma next to the component.

What comes back is usually a report plus a clean reference component sitting next to the old one, which is a very calm way to have an argument with your own library (and yes, I renamed my component to Pizza just to show you a fail):

The whole check runs through the MCP, and the answer is generated straight onto the canvas, next to the component it is about.

Three warnings:

  • Work on a copy. Never let an agent loose in a live library that other people’s files depend on. Duplicate first, test the workflow, then decide as a team.
  • Deleted variants do not come back. Every variant has a key underneath its name. Delete it and rebuild it identically, and the instances out in the wild still will not reconnect. Rename and repair, do not delete and recreate.
  • It still needs babysitting. On a real system with real history, this is assisted work, not magic. Go component by component, because the AI is quick and tireless and has no idea which differences matter. Once you are done, you can put a deterministic contract or other parity check on top that just checks whether things stay synced.

I use this technique for any sort of check, e.g. accessibility

Once you are aligned, you can do so much! Here’s an example: accessibility checks run in code, and then I get a little note like the one above in my Figma file next to the area with the issue and suggested solutions to discuss. Love it!

This is what becomes possible once Figma and code hold the same tokens and structure: Contrast measured against the real tokens, then laid out in Figma through the MCP

What if your product has more than one source?

Everything above assumes one. My sample is one design system in code and Figma on top, so that code wins and there is nothing to argue about. With two it still holds: pick one as the source, mirror it into Figma, keep the names matching on the other side. At three- iOS, Android and web- it falls apart, because each of them holds part of the truth and none of them is wrong.

You will not be the one deciding how that gets solved, and it decides what your Figma file can be, so it is worth knowing which one you are living in.

A library per platform. You do exactly what this article describes, once per platform. Each library mirrors its own codebase, like three small projects side by side. The drift then is not really between Figma and code any more, it moves into the structure: there is no single Button, there are three, and they slowly grow apart. That is the kind of thing a team ends up talking about as a whole, and it is good to see it coming.

Shared tokens, separate components. The one I see most often. Colours and spacing come from one source and land everywhere, while each platform keeps its own components, which is correct rather than sloppy, since a sheet is not a modal. You can mirror that split in Figma: one library for the variables and text styles, shared by everyone, and a component library per platform on top of it. The tokens are then safe to rely on, the component names are not.

One platform as the reference. Usually web. Then it is this article again, one mirrored library, and the others follow its names as far as they can. Worth knowing which platform that is, and if nobody can tell you, that is your answer.

Components defined as data. The one I find most promising comes from Nathan Curtis, whose talk about this idea I saw at SmashingConf Amsterdam in 2026 and really resonated with me. Instead of the definition living inside one codebase, every component is written down as data: its options, its allowed values, its defaults, in a plain file that sits above all the platforms. He calls it a contract (I wrote a longer article about contracts), and a schema says what a contract can contain. React, iOS, Android and Figma are all built from it and checked against it, so none of them is the original, and your Figma file stops being downstream of somebody else’s codebase.

Worth exploring, and not only for this. If you follow me a bit longer you will see JSON files and deterministic checks turning up everywhere, including in prototyping, which is where this way of thinking really pays off. So if you are working at that size, have a look at Curtis’s Spectacular (not a paid placement, as usual, just an honest recommendation), a Figma plugin and a command-line tool that read a component into schema-valid YAML or Markdown and render specs back into Figma.

The question to take back to your team is not which tool. It is which of these four you already are, and who is keeping it true.

What this does not solve

  • It needs a system worth mirroring. If the code is a mess, you get a beautifully generated mess. And the clean codebase you can happily generate from is rarer than any of us pretend. Mine behaves because it is a sample system I built myself. Real ones have two generations of components living side by side, props called type1, half the things undocumented, and a Storybook somebody set up in 2024 and stopped feeding. The honest version is that you do not need the whole system to be clean, only the component you are mirroring today, which is why I keep going one component at a time. And the first generated run is quite good at showing you exactly where the mess is. But yes it is work, a lot of work to get AI-ready.
  • Staying in sync is the open problem, and it’s tricky. My check tells me when the two have drifted; it does not stop them drifting, and I still trigger it by hand and in a playground. The state of the rest: Figma’s Code Connect links a component to its code but does not check whether they still agree, and it is on the larger plans only. Design system teams with engineers are building their own comparisons, which is the most common serious answer at the moment. Contracts are the most interesting direction and still early, closer to a proof of concept than something you install. And Figma’s own Code Sources (which they demoed at Config India in October 2026), which would point to the real system, is very promising, but still in closed beta. So if you feel behind on this, you are not. Almost nobody is doing it properly yet.
  • It only checks the structure. Names, properties, values, defaults. Not the visual side, no CSS. I am currently playing with this step; I will keep you updated. Contracts do not solve this either as far as I understand it: they can say which token a part must use, which catches most drift, and they cannot tell you whether the thing looks right when it renders. That is visual regression testing, a separate tool on the code side, and between Figma and code it is still me looking at two screenshots (the MCP compares them for me). There’s interesting work happening, but if I missed anything, let me know.
  • Library updates are hidden in Figma. This one caught me out properly. The library can be perfectly in sync and every designer still has to accept the update inside their own working file, and Figma buries that away in a corner. So half a team can be designing with last month’s Button, and nobody notices even though your setup is as polished as it gets.
  • It needs someone who can read both sides. Not write code. Read it, enough to notice when a translation went wrong. Still worth more right now than learning another tool.

Above all, this is also a human factor. All of this needs a change in workflow and mindset, on both sides. Designers have to read a codebase and to ask for access in the first place, which is the harder part. Developers have to prepare the system so it can be read, with typed props, descriptions and a clean manifest, and then be open about sharing it and inviting design in, which is the bigger ask. Nobody changes job, and reading code is worth more to a designer right now than another tool.

📖 Words in this article.

In-System Design (my term): designing with the system’s real components, on whichever surface suits the question, instead of next to the system in a tool that rebuilds it.

Props: the options a component accepts in code, like variant or size. Figma calls them component properties.

Token: a named design decision, likebackground-accent, instead of a raw colour value. Primitives are the raw values, semantic tokens give them meaning, and aliased means the semantic one points at the primitive.

Scoped (Figma): a variable is only offered where it belongs, so a text colour cannot be applied to a background.

Storybook: a website that shows every component of a codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the codebase rather than keeping its own copy.

Story: one example of a component, written next to it in the code. The examples you click through in Storybook.

Manifest: the component as a list. Every prop, value and default, written once, generated from the code. Storybook can produce one, from version 10 with the components manifest switched on.

JSON: a plain text file where every value has a label, so a machine can read it without interpreting anything.

MCP (Model Context Protocol): a standard plug that lets an AI connect to a tool like Figma or Storybook and read from it or act in it. Figma Console MCP (by Southleft) is the one I use for variables and library work.

GAPS.md (my term): a file where the AI writes down everything it could not express, was unsure about, or faked.

Skill: a packaged set of instructions an AI loads automatically for a recurring job. Powerful, and worth vetting before you install one.

Deterministic check: a comparison with no AI in it. Same input, same answer, every time.

Parity check (what mine is): a deterministic comparison of two lists, code and Figma, where code wins.

Drift: when the design and the code slowly stop matching, one small difference at a time.

Component contract (Nathan Curtis and others): a component’s definition held as data, above any one platform, that code and Figma are both built from and checked against.

Schema: the model that says what a contract is allowed to express.

Code Connect (Figma): links a Figma component to its code so developers see the right snippet. It links, it does not check, and it is on the larger plans.

Visual regression testing: screenshots of the real rendered components, compared automatically on every change, so anything that shifts shows up as a difference.

Variant key (Figma): the invisible id under a variant’s name. Delete the variant and the key goes with it, which is why rebuilt variants do not reconnect to instances.

In-System Design: a three-part series.

  • Part 1: Building an AI-ready design system: Code → Figma (you are here)
  • Part 2: AI prototyping inside your design system (3 November 2026)
  • Part 3: From code to Figma and back (10 November 2026)

About the author: Christine Vallaure

I’m Christine Vallaure. I design, I teach, and I spend an unreasonable amount of my time on articles like this one. Through moonlearning.io I teach Figma, design systems and AI workflows to designers and teams. Along the way I speak at conferences like Figma Config and Smashing Conference, mostly about where design meets code, and I am a member of the Awwwards jury.

title: Does Apple’s HomeView reduce effort, or ask for our attention?
text:
Does Apple’s HomeView reduce effort, or ask for our attention?

Truly useful domestic technology fades into the background. Too many smart home screens demand centre stage.

Apple’s latest foray into the home automation market is the HomeView, a 7 inch touch screen with integrated speaker designed to sit in a communal living space like the kitchen or dining area. It sounded pretty pedestrian, a competitor to Google’s Nest Hub or Amazon’s Echo Show, but something about it just felt a little off. Couldn’t the iPad already do most of this? My design brain kept asking, what problem is the HomeView solving?

The pitch: a shared screen at the kitchen table

I thought the best place to understand the intended use cases would be Apple’s ad for the HomeView. Light-hearted and cinematic, it takes the perspective of a family that places the HomeView literally at the centre of their kitchen counter/table, and their life unfolds around it at the pace of a manic start-up during a morning scrum.

This staging overlooks a real limitation that would typically relegate this device to one side of the room, wiring. The HomeView is a wired device and needs to be plugged-in to operate, this means having it sit neatly in the centre of a kitchen table or counter is less likely unless you have a kitchen conference table complete with grommets.

I understand an ad will always tidy up reality, but this tidies away where the device can live. Even if the cable were invisible, the premise itself surfaces a questionable design choice. The dining area is the one place families try to keep screen free, this is proposing we put one in the middle of it and make it a focal point.

It was here I reached for a quick test I use on any connected product, does this reduce effort, or does it ask for attention?

Good home automation disappears

Back in 1991, Mark Weiser a computer scientist at Xerox PARC introduced the concept of ubiquitous computing with a simple observation: “The most profound technologies are those that disappear. They weave themselves into the fabric of everyday life until they are indistinguishable from it.” [Weiser’s Scientific American article]

These ideas were developed further by cyborg anthropologist Amber Case, into the Calm Technology Principles, an approach for designing more human-centric technology. The first principle is that technology should require the smallest possible amount of attention. It echoes the test I use on any connected product. Against this standard, HomeView is working against itself, it falls into a classic design trap, assuming that visibility equals utility.

I’m not averse to a smart home, in a recent home refurbishment I installed a lot of ‘smart-tech’ from connected HVAC systems, lighting, CCTV, multi-room music and internet enabled appliances. All the ‘smart’ features are accessed through an Apple screen mounted discreetly on my wall, a 2018 iPad. Funnily enough with all this home automation, after the initial setup — most family interactions are largely limited to playing music and checking the doorbell camera.

Home automation is designed to be exactly that, automated not demanding constant interaction. It’s very much fire and forget, I want it all to just work for me. Once heating schedules are set up for the season I rarely have the need or urge to alter them, for more routine controls like lighting, I have pre-programmed physical switches and dials. By way of the attention test these reduce effort and ask nothing from me, whilst a dashboard in the middle of the room, inviting interaction does the exact opposite.

A centralised dashboard is very much a highlighted feature of the HomeView. In the Apple ecosystem the Home app consolidates all your smart home tech in one place, this unification is the key experience all these providers from Amazon to Google are seeking to deliver upon.

”…a classic design trap, assuming that visibility equals utility.”

In reality the experience is not as seamless, as third-party manufacturers typically provide limited functionality via their APIs to the Home app. The remainder of functions are then only available through their own app, resulting in a fractured two-tier experience. This can leave the Home app feeling more like a hobbled remote control rather than a fully featured control centre.

So an eight-year old iPad, using each manufacturer’s own apps can largely perform the home automation functions provided by the HomeView, which brings me back to that central question, what is the real problem being solved?

The real problem being solved

The HomeView is actually addressing two problems.

A manufactured problem

In 2022 Apple knee-capped the Home app features on the iPad such that it could no longer function as a home hub. Support for the old version ended in February 2026. Simply put, if you want to connect smart devices via Apple’s centralised Home app you’d now need some of their home hardware, specifically a HomePod or Apple TV, citing their new software architecture requires a device that’s always powered-on and fixed in the home.

This feature unbundling opened an opportunity for a single-purpose product like the HomeView, where previously a more than capable multi-purpose device like the iPad could have and did serve this need.

Missing out on the AI race problem

The other problem being addressed is Apple’s position in the AI race. They may not be competing for the frontier, but with no real horse in the race they are strategically positioned to act as the gateway for how households access third-party intelligence. The HomeView acts as a pervasive gateway, that deepens ecosystem tie-in all whilst delivering a series of revenue streams. A little investigation shows that accessing certain security camera recognition features requires an iCloud+ subscription.

A test for connected products

HomeView solves a number of strategic problems for Apple, just not that many real user ones. Herein lies the rub, a device that takes centre stage feels like it’s vying for my attention whilst not addressing that primary need of reducing effort.

“Home automation is designed to be exactly that, automated not demanding constant interaction”

Unobtrusive domestic user-centric experiences that borrow from the idea of ubiquitous computing are ones that fade into the background, and disappear into everyday life. These are the experiences that we can find most useful, demanding very little from us so we can focus our attention on things that matter more.

In a world filled with products craving our attention, we as designers can learn from the Calm Technology Principles and apply this mindful thinking to our own work, by starting with a simple honest question: does this reduce effort or does it ask for attention?

Further Reading

  • Designing with Tensions: Reframing Smart Home Ecosystem UX — ACM, 2026. Comparison of design frameworks used within Smart Home Tech.
  • Scaffolding a Design Process for Applying Calm Technology Design to Smart Toys — Interacting with Computers, 2026.
  • The Smart Home Agent Wars: A Five-Player Race Nobody Is Winning — Yahoo Finance, October 2026.

title: Who gets to name the future?
text:
Who gets to name the future?

Cracked, maxxed, and forward deployed: a field guide to AI’s boys’ club.

In a single meeting recently, I heard that someone had one-shotted a prototype, that we should spin up a tiger team, and that what the customer really needed was a forward-deployed engineer.

Nobody blinked. I nodded the way I nod at the dentist when he asks me a question with both hands in my mouth: agreeably, whatever, just get over with it asap, and with no idea what I had just agreed to.

It only hit me later, standing in my kitchen taking a bio break, staring into the fridge as if it owed me an explanation. I had just sat through thirty minutes of something that sounded a lot like a military briefing. About…software. Delivered by people whose most dangerous mission to date was a team offsite with a dinner spend limit that was going to make including alcohol difficult.

So I did what I always do when wording kinda tickles me. I went down the rabbit hole.

And ladies and gents, I found some good stuff.

Here’s what I found.

The AI era has a vocabulary. That vocabulary has a gender. And not just that. It also has a class and a color too.

It was coined by the same kind of people who coined the language of every tech wave before this one, and it’s doing what that language has always done: telling everyone else, very politely, that this room isn’t really for them.

Before you come for me in the comments: I’m not innocent here. I once titled an essay Designers, we should be killing it right now. I’ve told design leaders to pick one real fight a quarter and to spend credibility like money. I talk like this too. We all do. And there’s no vaccine for this one.

That’s exactly the problem.

Welcome to the war room.

The language of the AI era is borrowed from war rooms, Cold War think tanks, and Fortnite lobbies. Coincidence? I think not. Let’s take a look together.

Forward-deployed engineer. The hottest job title in AI right now: postings grew over 1,000% year over year heading into 2026. Palantir coined it in the mid-2000s for engineers embedded with US government and defense customers, borrowing the military idea of a soldier posted in the field, close to the action. Palantir’s first FDEs were called Deltas. As in Delta Force. Now OpenAI and Google are racing to hire them. Yesterday I saw an ad for a forward-deployed creative (turns out that’s just a sales guy).

Tiger team. The earliest documented use is a 1964 aerospace paper describing a team of “undomesticated and uninhibited technical specialists.” Undomesticated. Eh. The Apollo 13 rescue crew made the term famous. Today it’s what your VP says when a launch is on fire. Tigers, for the record, are solitary animals that spend a good part of the day asleep. I’m not saying that describes your tiger team. I’m saying the metaphor holds up better than anyone intended.

Red team. RAND, early 1960s. The red team played the Soviets, the blue team played the Americans. Every major AI lab now red-teams its models. Useful practice. Cold War name.

Blitzscaling. Reid Hoffman’s word for growth at any cost, built on blitzkrieg, the Wehrmacht’s lightning war. He has acknowledged the ugly echo and kept the name anyway. As someone who sometimes semi-identifies as German, I’d like to formally request that Silicon Valley return our words in the condition it found them. Keep kindergarten. Keep zeitgeist. Blitz comes home. Please and thank you.

Frontier. As in frontier model, frontier lab etc pp. This one goes deepest. In 1945, Vannevar Bush, who helped lead the Manhattan Project, sold postwar America on science as the endless frontier, a metaphor deliberately borrowed from the closing of the American West. The frontier is America’s oldest story about men going somewhere new and claiming it. The people who were already there rarely make it into the story.

I’m not loving what I’m finding so far, y’all.

Forget the locker room. Welcome to the Fortnite lobby.

The more ridiculous the terminology gets, the funnier its origins.

One-shotted. As a verb, it comes from video games, where it means killing something with a single hit. In AI-speak, it means a model nailed the task on the first try. (The adjective is older. Its first recorded use, in 1907, was golf. Hold that thought.) Tbh I’m almost glad it’s actually a golf reference and not some new porn kink I don’t understand. But still, I wouldn’t count golf as a class-diverse sport, so there’s that.

Cracked. As in we only hire cracked engineers. It’s Fortnite slang from 2019 for a player who is absurdly good, and it’s now the 10x engineer’s successor. At least one founder scrapped intern hiring entirely because no applicant was cracked enough.

When I was growing up, cracked was something that happened to a phone screen, or to a person after a long winter. Or, you know, someone being hit on by David Bowie:

Crack baby crack, show me you’re real.

Tokenmaxxing. Most of you will know this one by now. Burning as many AI tokens as possible to climb the internal leaderboard. Meta tracked it across more than 85,000 employees. The -maxxing suffix comes straight from the manosphere, where looksmaxxing was born. It’s leaving the tap running to prove how thirsty you are. Where’s the poetry in that?

996. Nine to nine, six days a week. A schedule China’s top court declared illegal in 2021, now openly advertised in AI job listings in San Francisco. Amelia Miller, who runs a platform for women returning to work, put it better than I can: 996 implies success only fits “a young, white male with an Ivy League education.” I hate this one the most for obvious reasons (hard-working mother of two).

The godfathers. Hinton, Bengio, and LeCun have been called the godfathers of AI since their 2019 Turing Award. When Fei-Fei Li got the matching title, she admitted she cringed, then kept it so other women would have a voice. In 2023, the New York Times published a who’s who of AI with twelve people in it. All men. I’m in the middle of a Sopranos rewatch and now have vivid metaphors of the top AI boardrooms. Every lab has its Tony. I’d like to know who gets to be Dr. Melfi, personally.

And then the two you’ve probably said yourself this week, which are sneakier:

AI native. A remix of digital native, coined in 2001 by Marc Prensky, who split the world into natives and immigrants. The claims were never backed by evidence, and Prensky himself later dropped the metaphor. It’s back anyway, with a new prefix.

Natives belong. Immigrants have an accent.

Notice who gets to decide which one you are. It’s rarely the woman who learned the tools on parental leave with a baby on her hip. By Prensky’s logic, my daughters are AI natives. They are also native speakers of whining, which has not once helped them find their shoes in one shot.

Creative technologist. The newest it title for designers and creatives who code. It grew up in advertising agencies, where one industry veteran summed up the people holding it: “in 99% of cases they were blokes.” Now the role is moving from the margins to the center of product teams, with the salary that comes with it. I have met many creative technologists. Every one of them owned a soldering iron and a strong opinion about hats. I’d love to see who gets the new offers.

That being said, I also spend too much money on hats, so maybe I should accept this one.

Here’s where I have to be honest.

My first version of this argument went like this: these words come from the military and the golf course, and the military and the golf course are white men. Case closed.

Then I checked. And, welp. It’s more interesting than that. I’d like to apologize to the golfers. (I’d like to, but I’ve seen the trousers.)

Today’s US military is not the boys’ club I had in my head. Women are 17.7% of the active-duty force, 32% of service members identify with a racial minority group, and 19.5% are Hispanic or Latino. Golf, the sport of country clubs, hit records in 2025: women are 28% of on-course golfers and people of color 26%, up from 8% in 1990.

Now put that next to AI.

Women are a bigger share of America’s golfers (28%) than of its new AI hires (26%).

And they’re hired into AI’s most coveted technical title, Member of Technical Staff, at 18%. That’s about the rate at which they serve in the US armed forces.

The golf course is diversifying faster than the AI lab. The army is about as gender-balanced as the frontier lab’s engineering floor.

If we’re really deciding the future now, I’d like that number to look quite a bit different.

The vocabulary isn’t borrowed from today’s soldiers or today’s golfers. It’s borrowed from a mythology: the officer in the war room, the Cold War think tank, the frontiersman, the clubhouse, the teenage gamer at 2 AM.

A story about who builds the future, written when the people allowed to build it were overwhelmingly white, male, and comfortable. The words keep that story alive long after the institutions themselves started changing.

That’s my actual provocation: not that every soldier or golfer is a white man. That AI picked its heroes from a picture of power that even the army has outgrown.

Tell me how that makes you feel. Please.

Some numbers to back the vibes.

AI is the best-paid corner of the job market right now: a typical AI posting lists about $177,000 versus $80,000 for everything else. Here’s who gets in.

Read that fourth row again. Women label the data. Men get the engineering titles.

And it’s not just who builds AI. It’s who uses it. Across 18 studies and about 143,000 people, women were roughly 20% less likely than men to use generative AI tools, and they were more likely to see using them as cheating. Even when researchers gave everyone equal access, the gap stayed. Ladies, why is our moral compass too developed?

On race, the most detailed public numbers I could find are old. In 2019, the AI Now Institute reported that just 2.5% of Google’s workforce was Black, and women were 10% of its AI research staff. That I couldn’t find anything newer and as specific tells you something too. It also sucks that basically all the data I can find is US-only. It might be better or worse elsewhere, but this highlights again that a lot of important AI work is done in the US, a diversity problem in itself.

Words ARE a door policy.

You might be thinking: Nicole, they’re just words. Relax.

Bullshit. I don’t believe in just words.

In 2011, three psychologists looked at more than 4,000 job ads and found that ads in male-dominated fields used more masculine-coded words, like competitive and dominant. When they rewrote identical jobs with more masculine language, women found them less appealing. Because they didn’t picture themselves belonging. Not one participant noticed the gendered wording. A later replication found the effect held in startups specifically.

Now look back at the glossary in this article. Deployed. Tiger. Blitz. Frontier. Cracked. Maxxing. Godfathers.

Every one of them tells you what kind of person belongs, and what you’re supposed to do once you’re in: dominate, conquer, out-grind.

That’s the whole point of a door policy. The bouncer never has to say no out loud. Not to me anyway; I’m crazy enough to get into Berghain, in case you couldn’t tell yet.

I won’t claim this vocabulary causes the gaps above. But I’d bet my pottery wheel it doesn’t help, and I love that wheel more than some relatives.

Women tell researchers they worry using AI looks like cheating. Meanwhile, the culture’s own slang celebrates being cracked and maxxing your way up a leaderboard. Something’s not adding up.

Remember the golf? Here’s the twist.

The paper that put one-shot learning on the AI map was published in 2006. Its first author: Fei-Fei Li. The godmother.

The phrase the boys now use to brag about first-try prototypes came from a woman doing slow, careful research into how machines might learn from a single example, the way people do.

It goes back further. During World War II, the US Army needed a machine to calculate ballistic trajectories: the ENIAC. Six women programmed it, with no programming languages and no manual, only wiring and logic diagrams. Their job title was literally computer (side note: can’t wait for humanity to come full circle and give us that cool-ass title back). When the ENIAC was unveiled in 1946, they weren’t introduced. For decades, photos of them were assumed to show models posing next to the machine. I really have no appropriate words for this one…so I'd rather not comment.

Women were in the war room. Women wrote the first code for it. But they didn’t get to tell the story. And they sure as shit didn’t get to name anything.

Other universes are available.

If we absolutely must borrow a world, and apparently we must, can we at least shop around? I tried on a few.

The gold rush. Honestly, the most accurate. Investors already call chipmakers the picks and shovels of AI. The rest writes itself: founders are prospectors, markets are claims, evals are the assayer’s office, San Francisco is a boomtown, and every pivot is a man knee-deep in a creek, insisting the next pan is the one. Love!

The catch: the forty-niners were mostly men too. The twist: women in the mining towns often earned as much as the miners, or more, by feeding, housing, and clothing them. Luzena Wilson sold a hungry miner her biscuits for five dollars, opened a hotel, and became one of the most prosperous women in the territory. Sucks for her husband though, he never found the mother lode.

Feeding, housing, and clothing the people who do the digging. In AI, we call that design.

Star Trek. Very promising. Instead of a forward-deployed engineer, you’d send an away team: same idea, nobody gets bombed.

The Prime Directive is basically an AI safety policy with better costumes. And Star Trek already did the thing I’m asking for. The original opening promised to go where no man had gone before. In 1987, The Next Generation quietly changed it to no one. A rename. On network television. Thirty-nine years ago.

The catch: Starfleet is, structurally, a navy. In space. With ranks. I’m choosing to look past it.

Star Wars. Honestly, tempting. Juniors become padawans, the staff engineer becomes a Jedi master, and vibes finally get the dignified name they deserve: the Force.

The catch, sadly, is right there in the title (wars). Also, every AI lab insists it isn’t building a Death Star, which is exactly what you’d say if you were.

The kitchen. I had high hopes for this one. Mise en place is context engineering. Tasting the sauce is an eval. 86 it is a deprecation notice. Then I looked it up: the classic kitchen brigade was designed by Escoffier after seven years as an army chef, as a chain of command. There is no escape. Even the soup has ranks for fucks sake.

The garden. My personal favorite, and not only because I’ve lost control of mine. You seed an idea, prune a model, graft one system onto another, compost the prototypes that didn’t make it, and accept that some things grow on their own schedule no matter how many standups you hold about them. Hallucinations are weeds: inevitable, and you deal with them weekly. The catch: nobody has ever raised a Series A on compost. Yet.

The pottery studio. I’m biased, obviously. You wedge the clay before you start, which is data prep. You center it, which is alignment, and anyone who has sat at a wheel knows centering is the hard part. You fire it in the kiln, which is deployment: the moment you stop being in control. And in pottery, cracked means exactly what it should. Something went wrong in the kiln.

What the good examples share is the thing the war room lacks:

They’re about making and tending, not conquering.

Nobody in a garden has ever been told to dominate the market. The tomatoes wouldn’t stand for it.

So let’s rename things.

Naming is design. And design is our job.

Designers, UX writers, conversation designers, researchers: we’re the people companies pay to decide what things are called. We name the features, the buttons, the error states, the career ladders. Many of us are women. We don’t need permission to walk into the war room.

We need to stop calling it one.

So here’s my proposal. Next time you hear one of these words, translate it.

The one I care most about is fluent. Native is something you either are or aren’t. Fluent is something you become. If the AI era has a door, I want it to say fluent so we can all get in.

The future is being named right now.

The AI era is being narrated, again, by too many white men. Not because they’re villains. Because they got to the microphone first (again, duh) and reached for the vocabulary they grew up with: the war movie, the space race, the frontier, the game lobby.

The good news? Language is the cheapest thing in the world to change, and one of the most powerful. Every one of us who names things for a living can start on Monday.

Women were there when the first computer was programmed. A woman put one-shot learning on the map. This time, let’s be in the room when the future gets its name.

Tiger team, dismissed.

Nicole is a Content Designer turned Design Director based in Stockholm, Sweden. She potters, writes poetry, and raises little girls in a house by a meadow. You can follow her writing here or get it directly to your inbox via her publication, eggwoman. Nicole is on LinkedIn. Find her portfolio at nicoletells.com.
